BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A ridge of high pressure will build over the region through the end of the work week. This will bring generally warm and dry conditions with above normal temperatures through Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures continue through next week. Record highs are possible, with temperatures 10-15 degrees above normal.
- A pair of weak systems will bring light rain showers to the area, one late Sunday north of a line from Baker City to McCall, and another areawide late Monday into Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Mild southwest flow continues as a strong upper level trough moves into western British Columbia tonight. The system will bring increased clouds and a slight chance of showers to an area north of a line from Baker City OR to McCall ID on Sunday. This system will provide enough mixing from southeast flow for mild temperatures to continue, with values in the low to mid 60s across the valleys. Monday will be dry as a shortwave ridge moves overhead, as another system moves across the NE Pacific into SE Alaska. A warm front will move across the Pacific NW and weaken on Monday, with a chance of showers areawide late Monday into Tuesday morning before drying out again. Precipitation amounts will be less than 0.10 inch.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A ridge of high pressure will build over the region through the end of the work week. This will bring generally warm and dry conditions with above normal temperatures through Friday. Most locations will see high temperatures about 10-15 degrees above normal, near record daily highs. For example, Boise has a forecast high temperature of 67F, with the daily record near 71F. By Friday, a deep trough will split and produce a cut off low pressure system near California, with a strong atmospheric river poised to affect the OR/WA coast. Some of the cooler air and moisture from this atmospheric river will creep into eastern Oregon and southern Idaho by next Saturday. This will bring slightly cooler temperatures with valley rain showers and high elevation snow. Uncertainty remains in the track of the cut off low and the strength of the atmospheric river which creates ample variability in snow levels and forecast precipitation amounts. Current forecast shows temperatures creeping back 5 degrees above normal with a 20-40% chance of measurable precipitation in southeast OR and southwest Idaho, with higher potential over terrain.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Thursday and through the weekend the ridge rebuilds over Colorado and does not budge at all, resulting in very little uncertainty in temperatures and precipitation chances through the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions are expected for at least the next seven days.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: GOES satellite imagery shows a few cirrus clouds moving south out of Wyoming in the northerly flow aloft. Other than that, it will be sunny, dry, and warm across the area with generally light winds. Highs should reach the mid 60s across the plains and I-25 corridor with around 50 degF in the mountain valleys and east slope foothills. Tonight's lows will be seasonally cool but warmer than average for early November with mostly clear skies and light winds. Looking at 30s across the plains and 20s in the mountain valleys.

A positively tilted ridge builds over Colorado Sunday through Tuesday. It will remain dry with above average temperatures. Ensemble temperature spreads from any ensemble forecast system are very small, resulting in high confidence in the expected temperatures across our area. An example is REFS for Monday has at most a 3-4 degree difference between the 10th/90th percentile maximum temperature at just a few northeast plains locations. The spread is less than that elsewhere. Needless to say temperatures across the plains will be 65-70 deg each afternoon. The mountain valleys/east slope foothills will likewise be warm with highs in the low to mid 50s.

Late on Tuesday models have a weak shortwave trough moving across the northern Rockies. GFS/GEFS are generally outliers with a colder and further south trough than any other modeling system. However, confidence overall is increasing that northwest flow aloft associated with the trough to the northeast will advect cooler air into our area especially by Wednesday morning, including a surface cold front. Ensemble guidance has essentially zero chance of precipitation with the trough/front passage across the plains, and it looks really dry aloft too such that for now we have keeping PoPs in the mountains below 10%, though that could certainly change as we get closer to Tuesday. West flow and cooler air associated with a trough is usually all it takes for flurries across the highest peaks/ridges even if models look too dry. Temps area-wide on Wednesday are likely to be cooler to some extent given the front and proximity of the trough, for now 4-6 degrees cooler is in the forecast. It's also likely to be breezy across the northern tier counties of Colorado later Tuesday into early Wednesday with northwest winds 15-20 mph gusting up to 30 mph. For now, it's looks cool enough that RH should not drop to red flag criteria. Thursday will also be breezy across the far eastern plains, but it does not look like we'll have any fire weather issues.

Thursday and through the weekend the ridge rebuilds over Colorado and does not budge at all, resulting in very little uncertainty in temperatures and precipitation chances through the weekend. It looks dry across our area with temperatures continuing to be 8-13 degrees above normal each afternoon.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Behind the departing clipper system, ensembles are in excellent agreement showing a highly amplified ridge building in over the Rockies Thursday into the following weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to just above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected through this weekend.
- Breezier winds return Sunday into Monday, however fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The upper level ridge is slowly canting towards the Intermountain West while being anchored off the West Coast. Currently high level clouds are moving through the region as a result from the trough moving through the northern tier of the United States. There is another low pressure system also pushing into the Pacific Northwest that will help center the ridge over the Intermountain west overnight. By doing so, the upper level low over Mexico will be cutoff from the upper level flow as our ridge creates a rex and eventually form an omega block over the Rocky Mountain Region. WInds will begin to pick up Sunday afternoon as the height gradient begins to tighten as the Low in the Pacific Northwest pushes against our area of high pressure. The Craig to Casper height gradient reaches a max of 45-47 meters Sunday and Monday so High winds aren't expected but wind gusts between 35-45 mph cant be ruled out. 700mb temperatures also max out between 6-9C Sunday afternoon warming the afternoon temperatures into the 60's and potentially low 70's for some areas. Consequently overnight temperatures will be a touch warmer overnight as well with temperatures in the 30's and 40's.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Warm and dry weather looks to continue for the forseeable future. On Monday, we will have a broad and fairly flat ridge positioned over the region. A weak surface front will creep into the High Plains and push up against the Laramie range, keeping light winds in place over the eastern areas, while those along and west of the Laramie range turn breezier. With 700-mb temperatures in the +4 to +7C range, we should see continued above average temperatures and overall pleasant conditions. A weak and moisture starved clipper system will traverse near the area on Tuesday into Wednesday. A few sprinkles or flurries will be possible, but only a small minority of ensemble members support any precipitation whatsoever for the region. Expect this to knock 700-mb temperatures down to the 0 to +2C range, while pulling the surface trough well east of the Laramie Range. This will allow breezy conditions to spread into the High Plains. Temperatures are expected to remain above seasonal averages, but with the cool down we should be a little closer to normal (perhaps 5 to 8F above average). While most will be breezy, high winds are fairly unlikely. In-house guidance shows probabilities around 20 to 30% for the typical wind prone areas.

Behind the departing clipper system, ensembles are in excellent agreement showing a highly amplified ridge building in over the Rockies Thursday into the following weekend. This feature will block or deflect any incoming storm systems, and push temperatures well above average once again. Since we'll be on the periphery of this ridge, temperature expectations are not too extreme. 700-mb temperatures around +4 to +6C are currently shown in the NAEFS mean, which is near the climatological 90th percentile. This isn't quite warm enough to support record highs, but expect temperatures at the surface to range a good 10 to 15F above seasonal norms. The strong ridge will likely also keep winds fairly light during this period.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Ridging remains overhead keeping warm and dry conditions in the forecast. The tail end of a weak disturbance will bring some high clouds to the northern valleys this afternoon before spreading to the Divide mountains this evening.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Warm and dry conditions will be the rule over the coming days.
- Some overnight fog is possible in the favored valleys.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Ridging remains overhead keeping warm and dry conditions in the forecast. The tail end of a weak disturbance will bring some high clouds to the northern valleys this afternoon before spreading to the Divide mountains this evening. Looking on satellite upstream these clouds are very diffuse...not a concern. Some fog may occur overnight thanks to efficient radiational cooling but coverage doesn't look too widespread. Sunny and dry conditions will also be the rule next week though a quick shortwave may move through Tuesday night into Wednesday bringing a few showers to the higher terrain. There's hardly any available moisture so if this wave does pan out, minimal QPF is expected. High pressure then moves overhead to end out the week with slightly above normal highs expected.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Just a note about the GFS being an outlier. It would bring isolated showers ot the Central Mountains mid week, and cooler temperatures to the Plains behind a stronger cold front.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and continued mild through the next 7 days.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...very nice conditions prevail across southern Colorado early this afternoon. Temperatures are warming through the 50s, topping out near 60 across much of the Plains. Winds are light and skies are clear.

Tonight through Sunday night...upper level high pressure will dominate the area through tomorrow night. This will lead to dry, quiet weather across southern Colorado through this period. Overnight lows tonight will off into the 30s across the Plains, and 20s for the San Luis Valley. High temperatures on Sunday will warm slightly with most of the Plains in the mid 60s. Lows Sunday night will once again fall back into the 30s for the Plains and 20s for the San Luis Valley.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: There is decent agreement among the model guidance, with the exception of the GFS. It tries to bring a shortwave trough across Colorado mid week, while the ECMWF, Canadian and ensemble guidance keep the system glancing by to the north and east.

Monday through Friday...for the most part, upper level high pressure will dominate the region through the work week. This will lead to dry conditions throughout the period. Temperatures will remain mild, with 50s and 60s across the Plains. The warmest conditions are forecast for Monday with a few low 70s possible. As mentioned above, a glancing shortwave trough will pass to the north and east sending a weak cold front across the Plains for mid week. This will cool high temperatures slightly on Wednesday, before warming back Thursday into Friday. Overnight lows will continue to fall into the 30s across the Plains, and 20s for the San Luis Valley.
Just a note about the GFS being an outlier. It would bring isolated showers ot the Central Mountains mid week, and cooler temperatures to the Plains behind a stronger cold front.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Forecast confidence drops substantively after Friday. Ensemble guidance suggests a cooler, wetter trend heading into next weekend, though around 35% of ensemble members still favor higher 500-mb heights and ridging next Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and increasingly mild weather will persist, with temperatures rising to 5 to 10 degrees above normal by Monday. Isolated areas of fog may develop late tonight in prone areas such as the Cache Valley.
- Model guidance suggests the next precipitation chances hold off until at least next weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Recent satellite imagery shows mostly clear skies across the region, with areas of valley fog quickly dissipating late this morning across portions of the Wasatch Back, Cache Valley, and Upper Sevier River Valleys. Building high pressure will bring stable conditions and a warming, drying trend to the region through at least Monday, with temperatures rising to 5 to 10 degrees above normal.

On Tuesday, a dry shortwave trough will graze across northern Utah, producing a minimal drop in temperatures by a few degrees alongside 700-mb temperatures dropping to around 0C to +2C from around +5C on Monday. This shortwave could also act to mix out any developing valley haze, though it's unclear whether or not the subtle mixing will be enough to fully mix out valleys. Afterwards, high pressure will return with temperatures rising once again through at least the end of the week.

Forecast confidence drops substantively after Friday. Ensemble guidance suggests a cooler, wetter trend heading into next weekend, though around 35% of ensemble members still favor higher 500-mb heights and ridging next Saturday.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Although avalanche conditions are generally safe, you'll still want to steer clear of stiff wind-drifted pockets of snow in the alpine. You are more likely to trigger an avalanche in wind-drifted snow on slopes that face the north half of the compass.
Continued weakening (faceting) of the upper snowpack will start to lead to small sluffs.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Most slopes hold too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around areas of firm, drifted snow if you find them below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe for travel. If you see evidence of recent wind-drifting on a steep slope or find a thicker slab at higher elevations on the north half of the compass, consider avoiding that terrain. Stiffer pockets of wind-drifted snow that could produce a small slide are common, like just below ridgelines and along gully walls. Most slopes near and below treeline hold too little snow to produce an avalanche.
